claim: Responsible research practices are practices researchers can engage in to enhance the transparency, validity, and trustworthiness of their work.
source: Responsible research practices are practices researchers can engage in to enhance the transparency, validity, and trustworthiness of their work (Steneck, 2006; Bouter, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scholarly work defining responsible research practices.

claim: Within biomedical science, examples of responsible research practices include open science practices such as openly sharing data and publishing open access.
source: Within biomedical science, examples include open science practices such as openly sharing data and publishing open access, as well as making the underlying methodology openly available, and explicitly acknowledging the limitations of the research findings (Iqbal et al., 2016; Moher et al., 2018; Wallach et al., 2018; Serghiou et al., 2021; Gopalakrishna et al., 2022b; Susanin et al., 2022; Roche et al., 2022a; Hughes et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to scholarly work.

claim: A pilot study distinguished three components for effectively socializing Ph.D. candidates into open and responsible research practices: role modeling, encouragement, and creating a psychologically safe atmosphere.
source: To effectively socialize Ph.D. candidates into open and responsible research practices, a pilot study conducted by a research team including the first author distinguished three components (Haven et al., 2022). First, the supervisor is supposed to be a role model, i.e., the supervisor engages in open and responsible research practices by for example making their own data and code consistently available. Second, the supervisor encourages the Ph.D. candidate to engage in responsible research practices. After all, it could be that the supervisor has more of a coordinating role or is perhaps versed in another sub-discipline than the Ph.D. candidate's research. Some have referred to this as the distinction between implicit (role modeling) and explicit (verbal instructions and encouragement) supervision (Fisher et al., 2009). Third, the supervisor is able to create a psychologically safe atmosphere where Ph.D. candidates feel the space to discuss dilemmas, admit mistakes, and question the status quo (Antes and DuBois, 2018; Antes et al., 2019a; Antes et al., 2019b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to a pilot study and other scholarly work.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scholarly work.
